title: Calm and Composed: The Pleasing Purr of an RX-7’s 1.3 Liters

body_markdown:
As a so-savvy car collector, I’ve long followed the personal mantra of “Buy high, sell low,” which began with my 1970 Ford Mustang Mach 1, for which I accepted $1200 as trade-in on another muscle car, then another, then a Ford Ranchero, then another muscle car… That trend ended when I voluntarily left the actual workforce to pursue a career in journalism. I’ve been poverty-stricken since.


I was looking more for a reliable daily driver than a sports car when I bought a used, few-years-old 1979 Mazda RX-7 off a car lot in Dallas. I was aware that I liked RX-7s, and the novelty of the Wankel-type rotary engine was intriguing. That was pretty much *all* I knew. That RX-7 was one of the most fun, dead-reliable, easily repaired cars I’ve owned, something I chalk up to pure dumb luck as a buyer.


Hagerty Marketplace/88Mazda


Odd how 100 horsepower seemed plenty back then. I held onto it until it became our second car, then our third, then something I seldom drove. I think my wife sold it to a friend.


That taught me a valuable lesson: Never sell a car you love to somebody who lives in the same small town you do. I met it at intersections for a year or two as I watched it slowly deteriorate, and I threatened to buy it back, like you would a cat you cared about that wasn’t being properly treated by a friend you gave it to. The cat, I did repossess; the RX-7, I did not. *Wish I had* —those are three words I’ve spoken so many times it would take all my fingers and all the fingers in your entire family to count. And I’m still saying it.


Hagerty Marketplace/88Mazda


I said it about my second RX-7, a red 1987 Turbo II that I bought when I was living in Michigan, from a pilot who flew for Kalitta Air, drag racer Connie Kalitta’s now-enormous, mostly-freight airline. It was exactly as the pilot described: Good shape, transmission snicks a little going into fourth, maybe needs paint. I promptly addressed that last issue with a trip to Maaco, which delighted me with what they accomplished for not much money, spoiled only when some vandal threw an egg at me at night, on a busy street, which landed on the still-drying hood and scratched it. Every time I got in the car, that scratch was directly in my line of vision. The car is long gone, but I’m still pissed.


Which brings us—finally!—to this week’s[Marketplace profile,](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/auction/1988-Mazda-RX-7/599e19ed-da35-4ae4-bc4f-e1e794d2bc8a) starring a black 1988 Mazda RX-7. Mazda’s first-generation of RX-7s, 1979-1985 models, are climbing up the resale ladder faster than a swimmer escaping a peed-in pool, but these second-gen, 1986-1989 RX-7s are still pretty affordable. (That’s something I never have been able to say about the complex, fragile, gorgeous, absolutely wonderful third-gen RX-7, one of which I “ *wish I had* ” bought from a buy-here, pay-here, former-gas-station car lot on Highway 90 in Bay St. Louis, Mississippi that, after two weeks of begging, disappeared the very day my wife said, “Go ahead and write a damn check!” Her words.)


Hagerty Marketplace/88Mazda

Hagerty Marketplace/88Mazda


Hagerty Marketplace/88Mazda


There were two legitimate complaints about the second-gen RX-7 when it first appeared as an ’86 model. One, it was bigger than its predecessor, causing many of us to just change the name in the speech we’d prepared for the 1979 Datsun 280ZX. And two, that the 1986 RX-7 looked sort of like a poor man’s Porsche 944. You heard that a lot back then, not so much now.


My 1987 Turbo II (quickly identified by the intercooler scoop on the hood, making that hood an actual target for thieves) had 182 horsepower, while the fuel-injected, twin-rotor 13B engine in this non-turbo Marketplace car was rated at 146. With its five-speed manual transmission, that’s still enough to put a smile on your face; with the automatic, maybe not so much.


Hagerty Marketplace/88Mazda


Wear points on Mazda rotaries are typically the rotor apex seals, and the what-were-they-thinking rubber seals that separate the coolant from the internals. Those rubber seals can go south, usually gradually, due to time and heat. Either seal’s failure can cause smoke out the exhaust (though a bit of it on startup isn’t unusual, especially after the car hasn’t been driven for a while). If you’re able to tell the difference between oil smoke and coolant smoke, it might be helpful when you’re considering a rotary. Other than that, the price for an excellent sports-car experience is mediocre gas mileage and an engine that is prone to oil consumption.


The seller became the second owner of the RX-7 in 2013, and according to CarFax, drove it only 3000 miles. The services performed during that period have been regular, with no serious repairs included in the listings.


Hagerty Marketplace/88Mazda


Hagerty Marketplace/88Mazda


Hagerty Marketplace/88Mazda


These RX-7s, especially the non-turbo models, are among that era’s most reliable sporty cars. And this one appears to have led a conservative, genteel life: Original parts are great, but if you’re buying this car for your 16-year-old, that reputation for reliability could be tested the first time there’s no adult in the passenger seat.


In number 3, or “good” condition, Hagerty values this RX-7 at $9400. The car appears to be close to number 2, or “excellent,” which may raise expectations price-wise, but if someone is searching for a kinder, gentler, sunroof-open, Sunday-afternoon cruiser, this ’88 RX-7 looks like a remarkably safe bet.


And my 1987 Mazda RX-7 Turbo II? Valued at (oh, man, *really?* ) $19,100 in number 3 condition. Pardon me, but I need a tissue and a moment to reflect on my life as the world’s worst car salesman.
